evidence.quote: נָאוֹר אַתָּה אַדִּיר מֵהַרְרֵי־טָרֶף׃ / “You were resplendent, glorious, on the mountains of prey.”

claims.explanation: The quoted Hebrew matches the verse; “resplendent,” “majestic,” and “mountains of prey” fairly render its wording.

claims.sentence: נָאוֹר, "made light, resplendent," is an odd form, and it sits one reshuffle away from the poem's key word: `nā-'ŌR` against `NŌ-rā'`, the same three letters, נ-א-ר against נ-ר-א.
claims.claim: נָאוֹר is an unusual form meaning luminous or resplendent.

evidence.quote: “Splendid, glorious. Enlightened.” Participle of נָאוֹר, Niphal of אור.
“נָאוֹר (‘resplendent/illuminated,’ Niphal of אור) is a near-hapax in this sense.”

claims.explanation: The lexical material glosses the form as bright, splendid, or glorious and identifies its occurrence in this sense as rare.

claims.sentence: נָאוֹר, "made light, resplendent," is an odd form, and it sits one reshuffle away from the poem's key word: `nā-'ŌR` against `NŌ-rā'`, the same three letters, נ-א-ר against נ-ר-א.
claims.claim: The two written Hebrew forms consist of the same three letters rearranged.

evidence.quote: Verse 5: נָאוֹר; verse 8: נוֹרָא.

claims.explanation: The written forms each contain four Hebrew letters: נאור and נורא. The excerpt’s comparison omits ו from both spellings, so it is not an exact account of the written forms.

claims.sentence: Some scholars emend it — that is, correct the text — to נוֹרָא, "awesome."
claims.claim: Some commentators or scholars propose reading נוֹרָא (“awesome”) instead of נָאוֹר.

evidence.quote: “Many commentators emend to נוֹרָא (Niphal of ירא, ‘awesome’).”

claims.explanation: The supplied research materials explicitly report this proposed emendation.

claims.sentence: The Alshich reports that the Aramaic Targum (the ancient Aramaic translation) already renders it that way, דְּחִיל, "feared."
claims.claim: Alshich cites the Targum’s rendering דְּחִיל for this verse.

evidence.source: Alshich (Romemot El), commentary on Psalm 76:5 (supplied research materials)
evidence.quote: “נורא כדעת המתרגם שתרגם דחיל את” (“awesome, according to the translator, who translated ‘feared are You’”).

evidence.source: Targum Psalms 76:5, as displayed in Mikraot Gedolot HaKeter ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/030908929502006506?utm_source=openai))
evidence.quote: “דְּחִיל אַתְּ אֱלָהָא” (“fearsome are You, O God”).

claims.explanation: The supplied Alshich entry explicitly attributes דחיל to the translator, and the Targum text contains that word.

claims.sentence: The Hebrew has "light," the Targum has "fear," and the poem has room for both.
claims.claim: The Targum renders the verse with a fear-related word.

evidence.source: Targum Psalms 76:5, as displayed in Mikraot Gedolot HaKeter ([journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/030908929502006506?utm_source=openai))
evidence.quote: “נְהִיר דְּחִיל אַתְּ אֱלָהָא” — the Targum includes both נהיר (“bright”) and דחיל (“fearsome”).

claims.explanation: The Targum does use a fear-related word, דחיל, while also retaining a light-related word, נהיר. The sentence is accurate as far as it goes, though the Targum includes both.

claims.sentence: Malbim shows why neither needs to replace the other.
claims.claim: The following description reports Malbim’s interpretation of the verse.

evidence.quote: “מפלת סנחריב היתה בלילה ... כאריה וככפיר היוצא בלילה מהררי טרף ... וקראו בשם נאור” — Malbim connects the night defeat of Sennacherib’s army with the image of God as a lion emerging at night and calls Him נָאוֹר.

claims.explanation: Malbim’s entry gives the nighttime Sennacherib-and-lion reading and explicitly explains the title נָאוֹר in that context.

claims.sentence: Sennacherib's army fell at night, so he pictures God going out from Zion like a lion hunting in the dark, and he explains the title "resplendent" accordingly: שלא יחשך לך בלילה בלכתך אל מחנה האויב, "for it does not grow dark for You by night as You go to the enemy camp."
claims.claim: Malbim links Sennacherib’s defeat to a nighttime lion image and explains נָאוֹר with the quoted phrase.

evidence.quote: “מפלת סנחריב היתה בלילה ... את ה' היוצא מהר ציון ... כאריה וככפיר היוצא בלילה מהררי טרף ... שלא יחשך לך בלילה בלכתך אל מחנה האויב.”

claims.explanation: The Hebrew quotation matches Malbim’s wording, and the English translation fairly renders it.

claims.sentence: The same night-logic drives the Passover hymn *Vayehi Ba-Ḥatzi ha-Laylah*, attributed to Yannai, the Byzantine-era Palestinian poet.
claims.claim: The hymn is attributed to Yannai, a Palestinian payyetan of the Byzantine period.

evidence.quote: “פיוט שחיבר יַנַיי” (“a piyyut composed by Yannai”).
“פייטן ארצישראלי מהמאה החמישית או המאה השישית” (“a Palestinian payyetan of the fifth or sixth century”).

claims.explanation: The cited source attributes the piyyut to Yannai and dates him to the fifth or sixth century in Palestine, within the Byzantine era.

claims.sentence: In Ashkenazi homes it is sung near the end of the Seder.

evidence.quote: “בנוסף נוהגים לשיר פזמון זה בסוף ההגדה בליל ראשון של פסח” (“It is also customary to sing this piyyut at the end of the Haggadah on the first night of Passover”).

claims.explanation: The same source identifies the Ashkenazic Haggadah tradition and says the piyyut is sung near its end.

claims.sentence: Every line ends on the word לַיְלָה, "night," as it lists God's victories that came while the enemy slept, Sennacherib among them:
claims.claim: The piyyut’s lines end with לילה and its subject is a series of nighttime deliverances, including Sennacherib’s defeat.

evidence.quote: “כל שורה בפיוט מסיימת במילה ‘לילה’, ונמנו בו נסים שנעשו בלילה עבור עם ישראל לאורך הדורות”; the text includes “יעץ מחרף ... הובשת פגריו ... בלילה.”

claims.explanation: The source states that every line ends in “night” and lists nighttime miracles; the cited Sennacherib stanza appears in the poem.

claims.sentence:
> הִפְחַדְתָּ אֲרַמִּי בְּאֶמֶשׁ לַיְלָה
> ...
> יָעַץ מְחָרֵף לְנוֹפֵף אִוּוּי
> הוֹבַשְׁתָּ פְגָרָיו בַּלַּיְלָה
>
> "You terrified the Aramean in the dark of night…
> The blasphemer plotted to shake his fist at the Desired [city];
> You withered his corpses in the night."
claims.claim: The Hebrew lines are quotations from Yannai’s piyyut, and the English renders them.

evidence.quote: “הִפְחַֽדְתָּ אֲרַמִּי בְּאֶֽמֶשׁ ... לַּֽיְלָה” and “יָעַץ מְחָרֵף לְנוֹפֵף אִוּוּי, הוֹבַֽשְׁתָּ פְגָרָיו ... בַּלַּֽיְלָה.”
It identifies אִוּוּי in the piyyut as “כינוי פיוטי לבית המקדש” (“a poetic name for the Temple”).

claims.sentence: The second half of the verse is a textual problem.
claims.claim: The following sentence reports a textual variant between the Septuagint and the Masoretic Text.

evidence.quote: “ἀπὸ ὀρέων αἰωνίων” (“from everlasting mountains”).

claims.explanation: The Greek wording differs from the Masoretic “mountains of prey,” so the verse does present a textual issue.

claims.sentence: The Greek reads ἀπὸ ὀρέων αἰωνίων, "from everlasting mountains."
claims.claim: The Septuagint’s corresponding phrase is ἀπὸ ὀρέων αἰωνίων.

evidence.quote: “φωτίζεις σὺ θαυμαστῶς ἀπὸ ὀρέων αἰωνίων.”

claims.explanation: The Greek phrase is quoted accurately; Greek Psalm 75:4 corresponds to Masoretic Psalm 76:5.

claims.sentence: That suggests the translator's Hebrew had הַרְרֵי־עַד, the phrase of Hab 3:6, וַיִּתְפֹּצְצוּ הַרְרֵי־עַד, "the everlasting mountains were shattered."
claims.claim: Habakkuk 3:6 contains הַרְרֵי־עַד and describes those mountains as shattered.

evidence.quote: “וַיִּתְפֹּצְצוּ הַרְרֵי־עַד.” The verse’s English rendering includes “The age-old mountains are shattered.”

claims.explanation: The Hebrew phrase and the English gloss are accurate. The proposed Vorlage for Psalm 76 remains an inference, as the excerpt signals with “suggests.”

claims.sentence: A count of the form מֵהַרְרֵי helps decide the question.
claims.claim: The following count concerns the form מֵהַרְרֵי.

evidence.source: Tanakh concordance search for מהררי, confirmed against the exact forms in the listed verses
evidence.quote: The exact form מֵהַרְרֵי occurs in Numbers 23:7, Song of Songs 4:8, and Psalm 76:5. Deuteronomy 8:9 is a substring-search false positive: its form is וּמֵהֲרָרֶיהָ.

claims.explanation: When exact forms are distinguished from substring matches, the count is three.

claims.sentence: It occurs three times in the Bible.
claims.claim: The exact form מֵהַרְרֵי occurs three times in the Tanakh.

evidence.source: Numbers 23:7, Song of Songs 4:8, and Psalm 76:5 (Masoretic text)
evidence.quote: The three forms are מֵהַרְרֵי־קֶדֶם, מֵהַרְרֵי נְמֵרִים, and מֵהַרְרֵי־טָרֶף.

claims.explanation: Those are the three exact occurrences. The similar form in Deuteronomy 8:9 is וּמֵהֲרָרֶיהָ, not מֵהַרְרֵי.

claims.sentence: One is Num 23:7, מֵהַרְרֵי־קֶדֶם, "from the mountains of the east," so the "ancient mountains" type is real.
claims.claim: Numbers 23:7 has מֵהַרְרֵי־קֶדֶם, translated here as “from the mountains of the east.”

evidence.quote: “מֵהַרְרֵי־קֶדֶם”; the verse’s translation renders it “from the hills of the East.”

claims.explanation: The Hebrew phrase and translation are accurate.

claims.sentence: Another is Song 4:8: מִמְּעֹנוֹת אֲרָיוֹת מֵהַרְרֵי נְמֵרִים, "from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards."
claims.claim: Song of Songs 4:8 contains the quoted Hebrew and the translation is fair.

evidence.quote: “מִמְּעֹנוֹת אֲרָיוֹת מֵהַרְרֵי נְמֵרִים”; the verse is translated “From the dens of lions, From the hills of leopards.”

claims.explanation: The Hebrew quotation and English rendering are accurate.

claims.sentence: That is exactly the pairing of den (מְעוֹנָה) and predators' mountains that vv. 3–5 of our psalm make.
claims.claim: Song 4:8 pairs a lion’s den with predator mountains, and Psalm 76:3–5 contains a corresponding dwelling/prey-mountain sequence.

evidence.source: Song of Songs 4:8 and Psalm 76:3, 5 (Masoretic text)
evidence.quote: Song 4:8: “מִמְּעֹנוֹת אֲרָיוֹת מֵהַרְרֵי נְמֵרִים”; Psalm 76:3, 5: “וּמְעֹנָתוֹ בְצִיּוֹן ... מֵהַרְרֵי־טָרֶף.”

claims.explanation: Both passages place dwelling/den language alongside mountain language associated with predators or prey.

claims.sentence:
אֶשְׁתּוֹלְלוּ אַבִּירֵי לֵב, נָמוּ שְׁנָתָם; וְלֹא־מָצְאוּ כָל־אַנְשֵׁי־חַיִל יְדֵיהֶם.
> The stout-hearted were stripped; they slumbered their sleep; and all the men of valor could not find their hands.
claims.claim: The Hebrew quotation is Psalm 76:6, and the English fairly renders its imagery.

evidence.source: Psalm 76:6 (Masoretic text and supplied English translation)
evidence.quote: “אֶשְׁתּוֹלְלוּ אַבִּירֵי לֵב נָמוּ שְׁנָתָם וְלֹא־מָצְאוּ ... יְדֵיהֶם”; the supplied translation has “The stout-hearted were despoiled ... the bravest of men could not lift a hand.”

claims.explanation: The Hebrew is the verse. “Stripped” is a defensible rendering of the first verb, and the remaining clauses are fairly translated.

claims.sentence: The first word is spelled like no other.
claims.claim: The exact form אֶשְׁתּוֹלְלוּ occurs only in Psalm 76:6.

evidence.quote: One occurrence: Psalms 76:6.

claims.explanation: The concordance finds this exact form only at Psalm 76:6.

claims.sentence: Where Hebrew would normally write **הִ**שְׁתּוֹלְלוּ, the psalm writes **אֶ**שְׁתּוֹלְלוּ, with an *aleph* in place of the *he*, an Aramaic habit.
claims.claim: Commentators describe אֶשְׁתּוֹלְלוּ as using aleph in place of the expected he-form הִשְׁתּוֹלְלוּ; the form is characterized in the supplied research as Aramaizing.

evidence.quote: “אשתוללו. הא' במקום ה' השתוללו” (“אשתוללו: the aleph is in place of the he, השתוללו”).
“Rare Aramaizing Ishtaphel (or Hitpolel) of שׁלל.”

claims.explanation: Both the aleph-for-he description and the Aramaizing characterization appear in the supplied sources.

claims.sentence: Rashi compares אֶתְחַבַּר, "joined himself" (2 Chr 20:35).
claims.claim: Rashi compares the form in Psalm 76:6 with אֶתְחַבַּר in 2 Chronicles 20:35.

evidence.quote: “כמו ‘ואחרי כן אתחבר ...’ (דברי הימים ב כ:לה) – כמו התחבר.”
“וְאַחֲרֵי־כֵן אֶתְחַבַּר יְהוֹשָׁפָט ... עִם אֲחַזְיָה.”

claims.explanation: Rashi makes this comparison and identifies the verse as 2 Chronicles 20:35.

claims.sentence: What did they do? Radak derives the word from שָׁלָל, "plunder": the plunderers became plunder.
claims.claim: Radak derives אֶשְׁתּוֹלְלוּ from שלל and explains the enemies as becoming spoil.

evidence.quote: “ואשתוללו מן שלל אומר כי הגוים אבירי לב שנאספו על ירושלים יהיו לשלל לישראל.”

claims.explanation: Radak explicitly connects the form with שלל and says the gathered nations will become spoil for Israel.

claims.sentence: Rashi derives it from שׁוֹלָל, "senseless" (Job 12:17): they went mad "like fools who err."
claims.claim: Rashi derives the word from שׁוֹלָל in Job 12:17 and interprets it as error or madness.

evidence.quote: “ונִגְזר אשתוללו מגזרת ‘מוליך יועצים שולל’ ... והוא לשון משגה ... כשוטים שוגים.”
“מוֹלִיךְ יוֹעֲצִים שׁוֹלָל.”

claims.explanation: Rashi cites Job 12:17 and glosses the expression as error or madness, comparing the men to fools who err.

claims.sentence: The army that came to strip Jerusalem is itself stripped, the reversal Isaiah curses in advance: הוֹי שׁוֹדֵד וְאַתָּה לֹא שָׁדוּד, "woe to you, despoiler, who were never despoiled" (Isa 33:1).
claims.claim: The quoted English accurately translates Isaiah 33:1’s phrase וְאַתָּה לֹא שָׁדוּד as “who were never despoiled.”

evidence.quote: “הוֹי שׁוֹדֵד וְאַתָּה לֹא שָׁדוּד ... כַּהֲתִמְךָ שׁוֹדֵד תּוּשַּׁד”; the supplied translation says “you ravager who are not ravaged” and then “When you have done ravaging, you shall be ravaged.”

claims.explanation: The verse says the ravager has not yet been ravaged, then predicts that he will be. “Never” conflicts with that prediction.
claims.suggested_fix: Change “who were never despoiled” to “though you have not yet been despoiled.”

claims.sentence: God in v. 5 is `'ad-**D**IYR`, "majestic." These men are `'ab-**B**IY-rēy`, "mighty." One letter separates the words and the power gap between them is total.
claims.claim: Only one letter separates the exact forms אַדִּיר and אַבִּירֵי.

evidence.quote: Verse 5: “אַדִּיר”; verse 6: “אַבִּירֵי.” The latter includes the plural-construct ending י.

claims.explanation: The base forms אדיר and אביר differ by one consonant, but the exact form in verse 6 is אבירי, which also has an additional ending.
claims.suggested_fix: Change “One letter separates the words” to “Their base forms differ by one consonant.”

claims.sentence: The sleep verb נָמוּ turns up in another anti-Assyrian scene: נָמוּ רֹעֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר יִשְׁכְּנוּ אַדִּירֶיךָ, "your shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria; your nobles lie still" (Nah 3:18).
claims.claim: Nahum 3:18 contains the quoted wording and addresses the king of Assyria.

evidence.quote: “נָמוּ רֹעֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר יִשְׁכְּנוּ אַדִּירֶיךָ”; the supplied translation begins “Your shepherds are slumbering, O king of Assyria.”

claims.explanation: The Hebrew wording is accurate, and the English is a fair rendering of the verse.

claims.sentence: Nahum, the Bible's anti-Assyrian poem, uses the psalm's vocabulary thickly elsewhere too: God גּוֹעֵר בַּיָּם, "rebukes the sea" (1:4, compare v. 7); he mocks אַיֵּה מְעוֹן אֲרָיוֹת, "where is the lions' den?" (2:12, compare v. 3).
claims.claim: Nahum 1:4 says God rebukes the sea, and Nahum 2:12 contains אַיֵּה מְעוֹן אֲרָיוֹת (“Where is the lions’ den?”).

evidence.quote: “גּוֹעֵר בַּיָּם.”
“אַיֵּה מְעוֹן אֲרָיוֹת”; translated “What has become of that lions’ den?”

claims.explanation: Both Hebrew phrases and their English glosses are accurate. “Mocks” is the guide’s interpretation of the rhetorical question.

claims.sentence: In Nahum the Assyrian nobles are called אַדִּירִים.
claims.claim: The exact form אַדִּירִים occurs in Nahum 3:18 for the Assyrian nobles.

evidence.quote: The verse has “אַדִּירֶיךָ” (“your nobles”), not the unsuffixed form “אַדִּירִים.”

claims.explanation: The lexical connection is sound, but the verse’s exact form includes the second-person suffix.

claims.sentence: It also sharpens a contrast with another psalm: הִנֵּה לֹא־יָנוּם וְלֹא יִישָׁן שׁוֹמֵר יִשְׂרָאֵל, "behold, the Guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps" (Ps 121:4).
claims.claim: Psalm 121:4 contains the quoted Hebrew and the English rendering is fair.

evidence.quote: “הִנֵּה לֹא־יָנוּם וְלֹא יִישָׁן שׁוֹמֵר יִשְׂרָאֵל”; translated “the guardian of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps.”

claims.explanation: The Hebrew and English wording match the verse’s text and sense.

claims.sentence: The sleep, moreover, is the kind no one wakes from: וְיָשְׁנוּ שְׁנַת־עוֹלָם וְלֹא יָקִיצוּ, "they shall sleep an everlasting sleep and not wake" (Jer 51:39).
claims.claim: Jeremiah 51:39 contains the quoted Hebrew and English rendering.

evidence.quote: “וְיָשְׁנוּ שְׁנַת־עוֹלָם וְלֹא יָקִיצוּ”; translated “sleep an endless sleep, Never to awake.”

claims.explanation: The quoted words and their translation match Jeremiah 51:39.

claims.sentence: The last clause has no parallel in the Bible.
claims.claim: The idiom לֹא־מָצְאוּ ... יְדֵיהֶם (“they did not find their hands”) occurs only in Psalm 76:6.

evidence.source: Tanakh concordance searches for מצאו ידיהם and כל אנשי חיל ידיהם
evidence.quote: The exact query “כל אנשי חיל ידיהם” returns Psalm 76:6 only; “מצאו ידיהם” returns no additional match.

claims.claim: Don Giovanni is a 1787 work with a libretto by Lorenzo Da Ponte.

claims.sentence: The psalm itself never does.
